claim: Perceptual decision making has been studied predominantly using tasks in which there is little ambiguity as to when observers should begin accumulating sensory information.
source: To date, perceptual decision making, described as the process whereby noisy sensory information is accumulated over time towards a decision bound, has been studied predominantly using tasks in which there is little ambiguity as to when observers should begin accumulating sensory information (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff and Smith, 2004; Shadlen and Kiani, 2013; Smith and Ratcliff, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on perceptual decision making.

claim: There are significant advantages to knowing precisely when sensory evidence will be available across a wide-range of perceptual tasks.
source: It has been documented extensively throughout the temporal attention literature, that there are significant advantages, across a wide-range of perceptual tasks, to knowing precisely when sensory evidence will be available (e.g. Correa et al., 2006; Jepma et al., 2012; Niemi and Näätänen, 1981; Nobre et al., 2007; Nobre and van Ede, 2018; Vangkilde et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to temporal attention literature.

claim: Mistiming accumulation onset can lead to false alarms and fast errors when accumulation is premature.
source: Such uncertainty presents a critical challenge because mistiming accumulation onset can have detrimental consequences: premature accumulation can lead to false alarms and fast errors while commencing accumulation late can lead to information loss and slow or missed responses (Teichert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teichert et al., 2016.

claim: Mistiming accumulation onset can lead to information loss and slow or missed responses when accumulation commences late.
source: Such uncertainty presents a critical challenge because mistiming accumulation onset can have detrimental consequences: premature accumulation can lead to false alarms and fast errors while commencing accumulation late can lead to information loss and slow or missed responses (Teichert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teichert et al., 2016.

claim: The Gated Accumulator Model suggests that evidence accumulation onset is contingent on sensory input surpassing a threshold level.
source: For instance, the Gated Accumulator Model, suggests that evidence accumulation onset is contingent on sensory input surpassing a threshold level (Purcell et al., 2010; Purcell et al., 2012; Schall et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Purcell et al. and Schall et al. studies.

claim: In a continuous monitoring context where the timing of target sensory changes are unpredictable, early target selection mechanisms are involved in triggering evidence accumulation.
source: Similarly, evidence from human electrophysiology suggests that in a continuous monitoring context, where the timing of target sensory changes are unpredictable, early target selection mechanisms are involved in triggering evidence accumulation (Loughnane et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Loughnane et al., 2016.

claim: The amplitude of target selection signals is heavily dependent on the strength of the sensory evidence.
source: However, the amplitude of target selection signals was found to be heavily dependent on the strength of the sensory evidence and therefore it is not clear how broadly such a stimulus-driven strategy can be applied.
evidence: Based on findings from Loughnane et al., 2016 study mentioned in context.

claim: The onset of sensory evidence accumulation may be subject to top-down control and adapted in accordance with the temporal context or demands of the sensory environment.
source: An additional possibility suggested by Teichert et al. (2016) is that the onset of sensory evidence accumulation may be subject to top-down control and adapted in accordance with the temporal context or demands of the sensory environment.
evidence: Supported by citation to Teichert et al., 2016.

claim: Prior knowledge of sensory evidence onset modulates the timing of accumulation onset.
source: In the context of temporal uncertainty, behavioural modelling and psychophysics studies have indicated that prior knowledge of sensory evidence onset does modulate the timing of accumulation onset (Bausenhart et al., 2010; Jepma et al., 2012; Seibold et al., 2011), while others have pointed to |effects on the quality of sensory information (Rohenkohl et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral modeling and psychophysics studies.

claim: The centro-parietal positivity (CPP) traces sensory evidence accumulation.
source: We traced activity in two previously characterised decision variable signals that trace sensory evidence accumulation: the centro-parietal positivity (CPP; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; Kelly and O'Connell, 2015; O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015) and effector-selective Mu/Beta band (10–30 Hz) activity (de Lange et al., 2013; Donner et al., 2009; O'Connell et al., 2012; Siegel et al., 2011; Steinemann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior CPP studies.

claim: Effector-selective Mu/Beta band (10–30 Hz) activity traces sensory evidence accumulation.
source: We traced activity in two previously characterised decision variable signals that trace sensory evidence accumulation: the centro-parietal positivity (CPP; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; Kelly and O'Connell, 2015; O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015) and effector-selective Mu/Beta band (10–30 Hz) activity (de Lange et al., 2013; Donner et al., 2009; O'Connell et al., 2012; Siegel et al., 2011; Steinemann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior Mu/Beta studies.

claim: The CPP builds gradually during decision formation at a rate proportional to evidence strength.
source: Each of these signals builds gradually during decision formation at a rate proportional to evidence strength, peaks around the time of a decision-reporting movement, predicts choice accuracy and RT across trials and exhibits amplitude modulations consistent with decision bound adjustments (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Steinemann et al., 2018; Loughnane et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies characterizing the CPP.

claim: The CPP peaks around the time of a decision-reporting movement.
source: Each of these signals builds gradually during decision formation at a rate proportional to evidence strength, peaks around the time of a decision-reporting movement, predicts choice accuracy and RT across trials and exhibits amplitude modulations consistent with decision bound adjustments (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Steinemann et al., 2018; Loughnane et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies characterizing the CPP.

claim: The CPP predicts choice accuracy and RT across trials.
source: Each of these signals builds gradually during decision formation at a rate proportional to evidence strength, peaks around the time of a decision-reporting movement, predicts choice accuracy and RT across trials and exhibits amplitude modulations consistent with decision bound adjustments (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Steinemann et al., 2018; Loughnane et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies characterizing the CPP.

claim: The CPP exhibits amplitude modulations consistent with decision bound adjustments.
source: Each of these signals builds gradually during decision formation at a rate proportional to evidence strength, peaks around the time of a decision-reporting movement, predicts choice accuracy and RT across trials and exhibits amplitude modulations consistent with decision bound adjustments (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Steinemann et al., 2018; Loughnane et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies characterizing the CPP.

claim: The CPP correlates strongly with subjective reports of stimulus intensity.
source: More recently, the CPP has been further characterised within the same decision theoretic framework for a diverse range of perceptual tasks (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018; Boubenec et al., 2017; Herding et al., 2019; Luyckx et al., 2019; Philiastides et al., 2014; Rungratsameetaweemana et al., 2018; Spitzer et al., 2017; von Lautz et al., 2019; van Vugt et al., 2019), has been shown to correlate strongly with subjective reports of stimulus intensity (Tagliabue et al., 2019) and predict the timing and probability of choice error signaling (Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tagliabue et al., 2019.

claim: The CPP predicts the timing and probability of choice error signaling.
source: More recently, the CPP has been further characterised within the same decision theoretic framework for a diverse range of perceptual tasks (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018; Boubenec et al., 2017; Herding et al., 2019; Luyckx et al., 2019; Philiastides et al., 2014; Rungratsameetaweemana et al., 2018; Spitzer et al., 2017; von Lautz et al., 2019; van Vugt et al., 2019), has been shown to correlate strongly with subjective reports of stimulus intensity (Tagliabue et al., 2019) and predict the timing and probability of choice error signaling (Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy et al., 2015.

claim: The evidence-dependent build-up of the CPP reliably precedes that of motor preparation signals.
source: First, the evidence-dependent build-up of the CPP has been shown to reliably precede that of motor preparation signals (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly and O'Connell, 2013.

claim: Premotor Mu/Beta-band activity contralateral to the decision reporting effector always reaches a stereotyped threshold level prior to response execution.
source: Second, it has been shown across several studies that the CPP and motor signals undergo distinct strategic adjustments: premotor Mu/Beta-band activity contralateral to the decision reporting effector always reaches a stereotyped threshold level prior to response execution but both contralateral and ipsilateral signals exhibit systematic shifts in their starting levels in response to prior information about time constraints (Steinemann et al., 2018) and stimulus probability (Kelly et al., 2019), as well as a temporally increasing urgency component to their build-up (Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steinemann et al., 2018 and Kelly et al., 2019.

claim: Contralateral and ipsilateral Mu/Beta signals exhibit systematic shifts in their starting levels in response to prior information about time constraints.
source: Second, it has been shown across several studies that the CPP and motor signals undergo distinct strategic adjustments: premotor Mu/Beta-band activity contralateral to the decision reporting effector always reaches a stereotyped threshold level prior to response execution but both contralateral and ipsilateral signals exhibit systematic shifts in their starting levels in response to prior information about time constraints (Steinemann et al., 2018) and stimulus probability (Kelly et al., 2019), as well as a temporally increasing urgency component to their build-up (Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steinemann et al., 2018 and Kelly et al., 2019.

claim: Mu/Beta signals exhibit a temporally increasing urgency component to their build-up.
source: Second, it has been shown across several studies that the CPP and motor signals undergo distinct strategic adjustments: premotor Mu/Beta-band activity contralateral to the decision reporting effector always reaches a stereotyped threshold level prior to response execution but both contralateral and ipsilateral signals exhibit systematic shifts in their starting levels in response to prior information about time constraints (Steinemann et al., 2018) and stimulus probability (Kelly et al., 2019), as well as a temporally increasing urgency component to their build-up (Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murphy et al., 2016, Steinemann et al., 2018, and Kelly et al., 2019.

claim: The CPP does not change its starting level.
source: In contrast, the CPP has been found to not change its starting level and its pre-choice amplitude varied systematically as a function of RT for discrete decisions with a time limit (Steinemann et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steinemann et al., 2018 and Kelly et al., 2019.

claim: The CPP's pre-choice amplitude varies systematically as a function of RT for discrete decisions with a time limit.
source: In contrast, the CPP has been found to not change its starting level and its pre-choice amplitude varied systematically as a function of RT for discrete decisions with a time limit (Steinemann et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steinemann et al., 2018 and Kelly et al., 2019.

claim: The CPP encodes a pure representation of cumulative evidence that is fed to the motor level where it is combined with other strategic influences.
source: Together, these data suggest that the CPP encodes a pure representation of cumulative evidence that is fed to the motor level where it is combined with other strategic influences.
evidence: Based on inference from the cited studies and their findings about CPP and motor signals.

claim: Subjects systematically initiated evidence accumulation in advance of the evidence when unable to time the onset of decision formation to coincide with uncertain onset of choice-relevant sensory evidence.
source: We found that in this situation where subjects are unable to time the onset of decision formation to coincide with the uncertain onset of choice-relevant sensory evidence (contrast change in experiment one or coherent motion onset in experiment 2), they systematically initiated evidence accumulation in advance of the evidence.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from both experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: Premature evidence accumulation was reflected in the build-up of the CPP during the foreperiod.
source: This was reflected in the build-up of the CPP during the foreperiod, which, in experiment 2, directly reflected random fluctuations in motion energy, and also in choice-predictive lateralisation of Mu/Beta band activity.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from the study.

claim: In experiment 2, CPP build-up during the foreperiod directly reflected random fluctuations in motion energy.
source: This was reflected in the build-up of the CPP during the foreperiod, which, in experiment 2, directly reflected random fluctuations in motion energy, and also in choice-predictive lateralisation of Mu/Beta band activity.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from experiment 2.

claim: Premature evidence accumulation was reflected in choice-predictive lateralisation of Mu/Beta band activity.
source: This was reflected in the build-up of the CPP during the foreperiod, which, in experiment 2, directly reflected random fluctuations in motion energy, and also in choice-predictive lateralisation of Mu/Beta band activity.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from the study.

claim: The timing of accumulation onset relative to the sensory change accounted for pronounced foreperiod effects on choice behaviour including increased miss rates on short foreperiod trials.
source: The timing of accumulation onset relative to the sensory change accounted for the pronounced foreperiod effects that were observed on choice behaviour including increased miss rates on short foreperiod trials and elevated premature responses and fast errors on long foreperiod trials.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from the study.

claim: The timing of accumulation onset relative to the sensory change accounted for elevated premature responses and fast errors on long foreperiod trials.
source: The timing of accumulation onset relative to the sensory change accounted for the pronounced foreperiod effects that were observed on choice behaviour including increased miss rates on short foreperiod trials and elevated premature responses and fast errors on long foreperiod trials.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from the study.

claim: Accumulation onset timing varied systematically according to recent trial foreperiod duration, with accumulation commencing earlier if the previous foreperiod was shorter.
source: Furthermore, we found that accumulation onset timing was not fixed across trials but varied systematically according to recent trial foreperiod duration, with accumulation commencing earlier if the previous foreperiod was shorter.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from the study.

claim: Choice accuracy was greater if the foreperiod duration on consecutive trials was congruent.
source: This also gave rise to a congruency effect whereby choice accuracy was greater if the foreperiod duration on consecutive trials was congruent.
evidence: Based on experimental findings from the study.

claim: Twenty-three subjects aged 19–30 (12 males, 11 females) were recruited for experiment 1.
source: Twenty-three subjects aged 19–30 (12 males, 11 females) were recruited to take part in a two-alternative, forced choice, contrast discrimination task as part of a study on perceptual learning taking place over the course of 6 separate experimental sessions.
evidence: Direct statement about the study sample.

claim: The final sample size for experiment 1 was 21 (10 male, 11 female; Age: M = 22.41, SD = 2.96).
source: This resulted in a final sample size of 21 (10 male, 11 female; Age: M = 22.41, SD = 2.96).
evidence: Direct statement about the final sample after exclusions.

claim: For electrophysiological analyses in experiment 1, two further subjects were excluded due to excessive blink and/or EEG artefacts (>40% trial loss).
source: For the purpose of electrophysiological analyses two further subjects were excluded, due to excessive blink and/or EEG artefacts (>40% trial loss), but their data were retained for behavioural analyses.
evidence: Direct statement about exclusion criteria.

claim: In experiment 1, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on RT (F(1.13, 22.56)=1717, p=1.68×10−39).
source: Taken together, our behavioural data suggest that subjects adopted a decision strategy that was more closely timed with respect to stimulus onset than to evidence onset. First, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on RT (Figure 1b–c; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1.13, 22.56)=1717, p=1.68×10−39), accuracy (Figure 1d–e; F(1.43, 28.64)=60.08, 8.91 × 10−13), missed responses (Figure 1f; F(1.07, 21.38)=114.29, p=2.88×10−17), premature responses (i.e. prior to sensory change onset, Figure 1g; F(1.01 20.12)=39.55, p=1.38×10−5) and points earned (Figure 1h; F(1.17, 23.49)=26.55, p=4.60×10−8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In experiment 1, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on accuracy (F(1.43, 28.64)=60.08, 8.91 × 10−13).
source: Taken together, our behavioural data suggest that subjects adopted a decision strategy that was more closely timed with respect to stimulus onset than to evidence onset. First, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on RT (Figure 1b–c; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1.13, 22.56)=1717, p=1.68×10−39), accuracy (Figure 1d–e; F(1.43, 28.64)=60.08, 8.91 × 10−13), missed responses (Figure 1f; F(1.07, 21.38)=114.29, p=2.88×10−17), premature responses (i.e. prior to sensory change onset, Figure 1g; F(1.01 20.12)=39.55, p=1.38×10−5) and points earned (Figure 1h; F(1.17, 23.49)=26.55, p=4.60×10−8).

claim: In experiment 1, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on premature responses (F(1.01 20.12)=39.55, p=1.38×10−5).
source: Taken together, our behavioural data suggest that subjects adopted a decision strategy that was more closely timed with respect to stimulus onset than to evidence onset. First, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on RT (Figure 1b–c; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1.13, 22.56)=1717, p=1.68×10−39), accuracy (Figure 1d–e; F(1.43, 28.64)=60.08, 8.91 × 10−13), missed responses (Figure 1f; F(1.07, 21.38)=114.29, p=2.88×10−17), premature responses (i.e. prior to sensory change onset, Figure 1g; F(1.01 20.12)=39.55, p=1.38×10−5) and points earned (Figure 1h; F(1.17, 23.49)=26.55, p=4.60×10−8).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In experiment 1, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on points earned (F(1.17, 23.49)=26.55, p=4.60×10−8).
source: Taken together, our behavioural data suggest that subjects adopted a decision strategy that was more closely timed with respect to stimulus onset than to evidence onset. First, there were significant main effects of foreperiod on RT (Figure 1b–c; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1.13, 22.56)=1717, p=1.68×10−39), accuracy (Figure 1d–e; F(1.43, 28.64)=60.08, 8.91 × 10−13), missed responses (Figure 1f; F(1.07, 21.38)=114.29, p=2.88×10−17), premature responses (i.e. prior to sensory change onset, Figure 1g; F(1.01 20.12)=39.55, p=1.38×10−5) and points earned (Figure 1h; F(1.17, 23.49)=26.55, p=4.60×10−8).

claim: A longer (1600 ms) foreperiod resulted in faster but less accurate responses and an increased tendency to respond prematurely in experiment 1.
source: Post-hoc tests (see Figure 1b–h; asterisks indicate significance levels) indicate that a longer (1600 ms) foreperiod resulted in faster but less accurate responses and an increased tendency to respond prematurely.
evidence: Based on post-hoc statistical tests of experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Short (800 ms) foreperiod trials in experiment 1 had slower and less error prone responses but misses were more common.
source: The opposite was true of short (800 ms) foreperiod trials where responses were slower and less error prone but misses more common.
evidence: Based on post-hoc statistical tests of experimental data.

claim: Overall performance in experiment 1 peaked on intermediate (1200 ms) foreperiod trials which yielded the highest levels of accuracy and greatest number of points earned per trial.
source: Overall performance peaked on intermediate (1200 ms) foreperiod trials which yielded the highest levels of accuracy and greatest number of points earned per trial with relatively low levels of both misses and premature responses.
evidence: Based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: The diminished accuracy on longer foreperiod trials in experiment 1 manifested specifically on trials with faster RTs, reaching chance levels for the subset of long foreperiod trials with RTs closest to the contrast-change onset.
source: This analysis revealed two key trends. Firstly, the diminished accuracy on longer foreperiod trials manifested specifically on trials with faster RTs, reaching chance levels for the subset of long foreperiod trials with RTs closest to the contrast-change onset.
evidence: Based on conditional accuracy function analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Responses made close to the target change onset in experiment 1 were based on little or no valid sensory evidence.
source: This observation suggests that responses made close to the target change onset were based on little or no valid sensory evidence.
evidence: Inference from the conditional accuracy function analysis.

claim: Beyond 2400 ms in experiment 1, accuracy diminished monotonically as a function of RT across all three foreperiod durations.
source: Secondly, the conditional accuracy functions also highlight that beyond 2400 ms, accuracy diminished monotonically as a function of RT across all three foreperiod durations.
evidence: Based on conditional accuracy function analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: SSVEPs are highly sensitive to modulations of stimulus contrast.
source: Key characteristics of these SSVEP signals indicate that they provide a read-out of the representation of the sensory evidence for contrast-based perceptual decisions: they are highly sensitive to modulations of stimulus contrast (Di Russo et al., 2007; Di Russo et al., 2001; Di Russo et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Norcia et al., 2015; O'Connell et al., 2012; Vialatte et al., 2010) and, their amplitudes predict both response accuracy (Steinemann et al., 2018) and RT (Loughnane et al., 2018; O'Connell et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior SSVEP studies.

claim: SSVEP amplitudes predict both response accuracy and RT.
source: Key characteristics of these SSVEP signals indicate that they provide a read-out of the representation of the sensory evidence for contrast-based perceptual decisions: they are highly sensitive to modulations of stimulus contrast (Di Russo et al., 2007; Di Russo et al., 2001; Di Russo et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Norcia et al., 2015; O'Connell et al., 2012; Vialatte et al., 2010) and, their amplitudes predict both response accuracy (Steinemann et al., 2018) and RT (Loughnane et al., 2018; O'Connell et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steinemann et al., 2018, Loughnane et al., 2018, and O'Connell et al., 2012.

claim: The SNR of the target SSVEP increased following the onset of the contrast change in experiment 1.
source: As expected, the SNR of the target SSVEP (corresponding to the grating whose contrast increased) increased following the onset of the contrast change while that of the non-target (grating whose contrast decreased) decreased.
evidence: Based on analysis of SSVEP data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The SNR of the non-target SSVEP decreased following the onset of the contrast change in experiment 1.
source: As expected, the SNR of the target SSVEP (corresponding to the grating whose contrast increased) increased following the onset of the contrast change while that of the non-target (grating whose contrast decreased) decreased.
evidence: Based on analysis of SSVEP data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There was a main effect of stimulus (target vs non-target) on SSVEP SNR in windows centred on 500 ms post-contrast change (F(1, 18)=13.93, p=0.002) in experiment 1.
source: Consistent with this we found a main effect of stimulus (target vs non-target) on SSVEP SNR in windows centred on 500 ms post-contrast change (Figure 2b; F(1, 18)=13.93, p=0.002) and 200 ms pre-response (Figure 2c; F(1, 18)=30.12, p=3.27×10−5).
evidence: Statistical analysis of SSVEP data.

claim: There was a main effect of stimulus (target vs non-target) on SSVEP SNR in windows centred on 200 ms pre-response (F(1, 18)=30.12, p=3.27×10−5) in experiment 1.
source: Consistent with this we found a main effect of stimulus (target vs non-target) on SSVEP SNR in windows centred on 500 ms post-contrast change (Figure 2b; F(1, 18)=13.93, p=0.002) and 200 ms pre-response (Figure 2c; F(1, 18)=30.12, p=3.27×10−5).
evidence: Statistical analysis of SSVEP data.

claim: Foreperiod did not affect the SSVEP SNR post-contrast change (F(2, 36)=0.06, p=0.94) in experiment 1.
source: Foreperiod on the other hand did not affect the SSVEP SNR (Post-contrast change: F(2, 36)=0.06, p=0.94; Pre-response: F(1 18.40)=0.01 p=0.92), irrespective of the stimulus (foreperiod x stimulus interactions: Post-contrast change: F(2, 36)=0.45, p=0.64; Pre-response: F(1.05, 18.96)=0.13, p=0.73).
evidence: Statistical analysis of SSVEP data.

claim: Foreperiod did not affect the SSVEP SNR pre-response (F(1 18.40)=0.01 p=0.92) in experiment 1.
source: Foreperiod on the other hand did not affect the SSVEP SNR (Post-contrast change: F(2, 36)=0.06, p=0.94; Pre-response: F(1 18.40)=0.01 p=0.92), irrespective of the stimulus (foreperiod x stimulus interactions: Post-contrast change: F(2, 36)=0.45, p=0.64; Pre-response: F(1.05, 18.96)=0.13, p=0.73).
evidence: Statistical analysis of SSVEP data.

claim: The representation of sensory evidence was stable across the three foreperiods in experiment 1.
source: Together these findings indicate that the representation of sensory evidence was stable across the three foreperiods and could not account for the observed behavioural trends.
evidence: Inference from SSVEP analysis results.

claim: On longer foreperiod trials in experiment 1, significant CPP build-up was observed prior to the onset of the contrast change.
source: Figure 3b shows that, on longer foreperiod trials, significant CPP build-up was observed prior to the onset of the contrast change (Figure 3b; one-sample t-tests: 800 ms: t(18)=1.79, p=0.14; 1200 ms: t(18)=3.71 p=0.0016; 1600 ms t(18)=5.52, p=2×10−5; correct and error responses pooled).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was significant pre-evidence build-up of the CPP on longer foreperiod trials as early as session one in experiment 1.
source: In fact, there was significant pre-evidence build-up of the CPP on longer foreperiod trials as early as session one (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; t(18)=4.12, p=6.4×10-5) and the amount of pre-evidence CPP-build up did not vary systematically across training sessions (main effect of session: F(4, 72)=1.18, p=0.33).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP data across sessions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amount of pre-evidence CPP-build up did not vary systematically across training sessions in experiment 1 (F(4, 72)=1.18, p=0.33).
source: In fact, there was significant pre-evidence build-up of the CPP on longer foreperiod trials as early as session one (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; t(18)=4.12, p=6.4×10-5) and the amount of pre-evidence CPP-build up did not vary systematically across training sessions (main effect of session: F(4, 72)=1.18, p=0.33).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP data across sessions.

claim: The CPP amplitude prior to evidence onset was larger on longer foreperiod trials in experiment 1 (F(1.27, 22.91 = 25.00, p=1.6×10−5).
source: Our analyses found that the CPP amplitude prior to evidence onset was larger on longer foreperiod trials (F(1.27, 22.91 = 25.00, p=1.6×10−5; linear contrast: p=4.75×10−5; quadratic contrast: p=0.17).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP amplitude data.

claim: There was an inverse relationship between the amount of pre-evidence CPP build up and RT in experiment 1 (F(5, 90)=6.56, p=3×10−5).
source: Moreover, there was an inverse relationship between the amount of pre-evidence CPP build up and RT (Figure 3d; F(5, 90)=6.56, p=3×10−5), irrespective of foreperiod duration (RT x foreperiod interaction: F(5.33, 95.91)=1.07, p=0.39), indicating that greater pre-evidence CPP build-up was associated with faster responses.
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP-RT relationship shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Greater pre-evidence CPP build-up was associated with faster responses in experiment 1.
source: Moreover, there was an inverse relationship between the amount of pre-evidence CPP build up and RT (Figure 3d; F(5, 90)=6.56, p=3×10−5), irrespective of foreperiod duration (RT x foreperiod interaction: F(5.33, 95.91)=1.07, p=0.39), indicating that greater pre-evidence CPP build-up was associated with faster responses.
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis of CPP-RT relationship.

claim: The build-up rate of the CPP during the foreperiod predicted RT, irrespective of foreperiod duration in experiment 1 (F(5, 90)=4.42, p=0.001).
source: Further, the build-up rate of the CPP during the foreperiod (measured as the slope of a line fit to the CPP waveform between −250 ms and 50 ms relative to the contrast change) also predicted RT, irrespective of foreperiod duration (Figure 3f; main effect of RT: F(5, 90)=4.42, p=0.001; main effect of foreperiod: F(2,36)=2.39, p=0.11; RT x foreperiod interaction: F(4.81 86.54)=0.63, p=0.67).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP slope-RT relationship shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Subjects in experiment 1 were 4.17 times more likely to choose left when responding prematurely (<150 ms; t(18)=3.20, p=0.005).
source: Subjects were 4.17 times more likely to choose left when responding prematurely (<150 ms; t(18)=3.20, p=0.005; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), 1.95 times more likely to respond left when responding quickly (<500 ms; t(20)=5.62, p=0.1.69−4; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and had faster RTs when left targets were presented (F(1, 20)=63.65, p=1.22−7; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Statistical analysis of choice bias data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subjects in experiment 1 were 1.95 times more likely to respond left when responding quickly (<500 ms; t(20)=5.62, p=0.1.69−4).
source: Subjects were 4.17 times more likely to choose left when responding prematurely (<150 ms; t(18)=3.20, p=0.005; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), 1.95 times more likely to respond left when responding quickly (<500 ms; t(20)=5.62, p=0.1.69−4; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and had faster RTs when left targets were presented (F(1, 20)=63.65, p=1.22−7; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Statistical analysis of choice bias data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subjects in experiment 1 had faster RTs when left targets were presented (F(1, 20)=63.65, p=1.22−7).
source: Subjects were 4.17 times more likely to choose left when responding prematurely (<150 ms; t(18)=3.20, p=0.005; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), 1.95 times more likely to respond left when responding quickly (<500 ms; t(20)=5.62, p=0.1.69−4; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and had faster RTs when left targets were presented (F(1, 20)=63.65, p=1.22−7; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Statistical analysis of RT data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The systematic bias toward left choices in experiment 1 can be attributed to the difference in flicker frequency between left (20 Hz) and right-tilted (25 Hz) gratings.
source: This systematic bias can be attributed to the difference in flicker frequency between left (20 Hz) and right-tilted (25 Hz) gratings.
evidence: Inference based on psychophysical research cited in the next sentence.

claim: Within the range of 20-25 Hz, the perceived brightness and contrast of flickering stimuli diminishes as a function of flicker frequency, even when they are matched in terms of physical contrast and luminance.
source: Psychophysical research has previously shown that within this range the perceived brightness (Bartley, 1938; Bartley, 1951; Wu et al., 1996) and contrast (Solomon and Tyler, 2018) of flickering stimuli diminishes as a function of flicker frequency, even when they are matched in terms of physical contrast and luminance.
evidence: Supported by citations to psychophysical research.

claim: There was significant pre-evidence Mu/Beta lateralisation on longer foreperiod trials in experiment 1 (1200 ms: t(18)=-3.64, p=0.002; 1600 ms: t(18)=-3.91 p=0.001).
source: This analysis indicated that there was significant pre-evidence Mu/Beta lateralisation on longer foreperiod trials (Figure 3i inset; one-sample t-tests: 800 ms: t(18)=-1.27, p=0.22; 1200 ms: t(18)=-3.64, p=0.002; 1600 ms: t(18)=-3.91 p=0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta lateralisation data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Longer foreperiods gave rise to greater pre-evidence Mu/Beta lateralisation in experiment 1 (F(2, 36)=3.64, p=0.04).
source: Similar to the CPP, longer foreperiods gave rise to greater pre-evidence Mu/Beta lateralisation (F(2, 36)=3.64, p=0.04) which in turn scaled inversely with RT, irrespective of foreperiod duration (Figure 3k; main effect of RT: F(5, 90)=2.94, p=0.017; RT x foreperiod interaction: F(5.22, 93.99)=1.68, p=0.14).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta lateralisation data shown in Figure 3k.

claim: Pre-evidence Mu/Beta lateralisation scaled inversely with RT, irrespective of foreperiod duration in experiment 1 (F(5, 90)=2.94, p=0.017).
source: Similar to the CPP, longer foreperiods gave rise to greater pre-evidence Mu/Beta lateralisation (F(2, 36)=3.64, p=0.04) which in turn scaled inversely with RT, irrespective of foreperiod duration (Figure 3k; main effect of RT: F(5, 90)=2.94, p=0.017; RT x foreperiod interaction: F(5.22, 93.99)=1.68, p=0.14).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta lateralisation-RT relationship.

claim: Greater choice-selective motor preparation during the pre-evidence foreperiod predicted faster RTs in experiment 1.
source: Thus greater choice-selective motor preparation during the pre-evidence foreperiod predicted faster RTs.
evidence: Inference from Mu/Beta lateralisation analysis.

claim: The rate of Mu/Beta lateralisation during the foreperiod predicted RT irrespective of foreperiod duration in experiment 1 (F(5, 90)=3.56, p=0.006).
source: In addition, the rate of Mu/Beta lateralisation during the foreperiod (also measured as the slope of a line fit to the Mu/Beta lateralisation waveform between −250 ms and 50 relative to evidence onset) predicted RT irrespective of foreperiod duration (Figure 3m; main effect of RT: F(5, 90)=3.56, p=0.006; main effect of foreperiod: F(2, 36)=0.47, p=0.63; RT x foreperiod interaction: F(4.82, 86.70)=1.45, p=0.22).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta lateralisation slope-RT relationship shown in Figure 3m.

claim: The CPP amplitude prior to response did not vary as a function of foreperiod duration in experiment 1 (F(2, 36)=0.47,p=0.63).
source: Figure 3g shows that when the foreperiod was short, faster RTs were associated with steeper pre-response CPP slope, in line with previous observations (e.g. Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012). By comparison, the opposite was true of long foreperiod trials where faster responses were associated with shallower pre-response CPP slope. The shallower build-up rate of the pre-response CPP on faster RT trials can be explained in light of the close temporal proximity of these responses to the timing of the contrast change and hence the lesser contribution of valid sensory evidence to those decisions.
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP amplitude data.

claim: The CPP amplitude prior to response did not vary as a function of response time in experiment 1 (F(5, 90)=0.64, p=0.67).
source: Here, however, we did not find any variation in the CPP amplitude prior to response as a function of foreperiod duration (F(2, 36)=0.47,p=0.63; Figure 3c) or response time (F(5, 90)=0.64, p=0.67; Figure 3e).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP amplitude data shown in Figure 3c and 3e.

claim: The amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of foreperiod duration in experiment 1 (F(2, 36)=0.49, p=0.63).
source: Similarly, the amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of foreperiod duration (Figure 3j; F(2, 36)=0.49, p=0.63) or response time (Figure 3n; F(2.16, 38.95)=1.80, p=0.18), consistent with a time-invariant action-triggering threshold at the motor level (Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta amplitude data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of response time in experiment 1 (F(2.16, 38.95)=1.80, p=0.18).
source: Similarly, the amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of foreperiod duration (Figure 3j; F(2, 36)=0.49, p=0.63) or response time (Figure 3n; F(2.16, 38.95)=1.80, p=0.18), consistent with a time-invariant action-triggering threshold at the motor level (Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta amplitude data.

claim: Ipsilateral Mu/Beta prior to response was more desynchronised on slower RT trials in experiment 1 (F(1.86, 33.40)=6.50, p=3×10−5).
source: By comparison, ipsilateral Mu/Beta prior to response, though not modulated significantly by foreperiod duration (F(1.46, 26.30)=2.82, p=0.09), was more desynchronised prior to response on slower RT trials (F(1.86, 33.40)=6.50, p=3×10−5) reflecting more preparation of the unchosen response hand on these trials and a closer 'race' between the alternative outcomes.
evidence: Statistical analysis of ipsilateral Mu/Beta data.

claim: Mu-beta lateralisation prior to response was stronger on faster response trials in experiment 1 (F(2.68, 48.31)=3.99, p=0.01).
source: Correspondingly, mu-beta lateralisation prior to response was stronger on faster response trials (F(2.68, 48.31)=3.99, p=0.01), a finding that is consistent with previous studies (Murphy et al., 2016).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta lateralisation data, consistent with prior studies.

claim: In experiment 1, subjects were unable to align the onset of decision formation to sensory evidence onset in the absence of foreknowledge about the precise onset timing of a subtle goal relevant sensory change.
source: The key results from experiment one show that in the absence of foreknowledge about the precise onset timing of a subtle goal relevant sensory change, subjects were unable to align the onset of decision formation to sensory evidence onset.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings.

claim: On longer foreperiod trials in experiment 1, subjects consistently commenced decision formation before the target contrast change occurred, resulting in a higher incidence of false alarms and fast errors.
source: On longer foreperiod trials, subjects consistently commenced decision formation before the target contrast change occurred, resulting in a higher incidence of false alarms and fast errors.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings.

claim: The premature onset of the decision process in experiment 1 was reflected in the build-up of the CPP and the emergence of choice predictive Mu/Beta lateralisation during the foreperiod.
source: The premature onset of the decision process was reflected in the build-up of the CPP and the emergence of choice predictive Mu/Beta lateralisation during the foreperiod.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings.

claim: Nineteen subjects aged 18–37 (M = 25.74, SD = 5.92; 10 females, nine males) were recruited for experiment 2.
source: Nineteen subjects aged 18–37 (M = 25.74, SD = 5.92; 10 females, nine males) were recruited to take part in a dot motion discrimination task comprising a single session of data collection.
evidence: Direct statement about the study sample.

claim: In experiment 2, there were significant effects of foreperiod on RT (F(1.07, 19.20)=150.60, p=1×10−10).
source: As in experiment 1, we first analysed behaviour separated according to foreperiod duration (summarised in Figure 4b–h) and observed highly similar trends including significant effects on RT (Figure 4b–c; F(1.07, 19.20)=150.60, p=1×10−10), accuracy (Figure 4d–e; F(1.47, 26.38)=7.69, p=0.005), miss rate (Figure 4f; F(1.08, 19.42)=63.76, p=9.7×10−8), premature response rate (Figure 4g; F(1.08, 19.40)=58.80, p=1.8×10−7) and points earned per trial (Figure 4h; F(142, 25.50)=10.10, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In experiment 2, there were significant effects of foreperiod on accuracy (F(1.47, 26.38)=7.69, p=0.005).
source: As in experiment 1, we first analysed behaviour separated according to foreperiod duration (summarised in Figure 4b–h) and observed highly similar trends including significant effects on RT (Figure 4b–c; F(1.07, 19.20)=150.60, p=1×10−10), accuracy (Figure 4d–e; F(1.47, 26.38)=7.69, p=0.005), miss rate (Figure 4f; F(1.08, 19.42)=63.76, p=9.7×10−8), premature response rate (Figure 4g; F(1.08, 19.40)=58.80, p=1.8×10−7) and points earned per trial (Figure 4h; F(142, 25.50)=10.10, p=0.002).

source: As in experiment 1, we first analysed behaviour separated according to foreperiod duration (summarised in Figure 4b–h) and observed highly similar trends including significant effects on RT (Figure 4b–c; F(1.07, 19.20)=150.60, p=1×10−10), accuracy (Figure 4d–e; F(1.47, 26.38)=7.69, p=0.005), miss rate (Figure 4f; F(1.08, 19.42)=63.76, p=9.7×10−8), premature response rate (Figure 4g; F(1.08, 19.40)=58.80, p=1.8×10−7) and points earned per trial (Figure 4h; F(142, 25.50)=10.10, p=0.002).

evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data.

source: As in experiment 1, we first analysed behaviour separated according to foreperiod duration (summarised in Figure 4b–h) and observed highly similar trends including significant effects on RT (Figure 4b–c; F(1.07, 19.20)=150.60, p=1×10−10), accuracy (Figure 4d–e; F(1.47, 26.38)=7.69, p=0.005), miss rate (Figure 4f; F(1.08, 19.42)=63.76, p=9.7×10−8), premature response rate (Figure 4g; F(1.08, 19.40)=58.80, p=1.8×10−7) and points earned per trial (Figure 4h; F(142, 25.50)=10.10, p=0.002).

claim: In experiment 2, there was significant build-up of the CPP prior to the onset of the coherent motion for longer foreperiod trials (1200 ms: t(17)=2.28, p=0.03; 1600 ms: t(17)=3.49, p=0.003).
source: As before, there was significant build-up of the CPP prior to the onset of the coherent motion (Figure 5b) for longer foreperiod trials (one-sample t-tests: 800 ms: t(17)=1.21 p=0.24; 1200 ms: t(17)=2.28, p=0.03; 1600 ms: t(17)=3.49, p=0.003), with longer pre-evidence foreperiods resulting in larger CPP amplitudes at the time of coherent motion onset (F(2, 34)=5.45, p=0.009).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: In experiment 2, longer pre-evidence foreperiods resulted in larger CPP amplitudes at the time of coherent motion onset (F(2, 34)=5.45, p=0.009).
source: As before, there was significant build-up of the CPP prior to the onset of the coherent motion (Figure 5b) for longer foreperiod trials (one-sample t-tests: 800 ms: t(17)=1.21 p=0.24; 1200 ms: t(17)=2.28, p=0.03; 1600 ms: t(17)=3.49, p=0.003), with longer pre-evidence foreperiods resulting in larger CPP amplitudes at the time of coherent motion onset (F(2, 34)=5.45, p=0.009).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP amplitude data.

claim: In experiment 2, there was significant pre-evidence Mu/Beta lateralisation on longer foreperiod trials (1600 ms: t(17)=-3.23, p=0.005).
source: Similarly, we observed desynchronisation in Mu/Beta band activity over the hemispheres contralateral and ipsilateral to the response-executing hand throughout the pre-evidence foreperiod, with a progressive lateralisation toward the contralateral hemisphere on longer foreperiod trials (Figure 5i; 800 ms t(17)=-.40, p=0.69; 1200 ms: t(17)=-1.65, p=0.12; 1600 ms: t(17)=-3.23, p=0.005; main effect of foreperiod: F(3, 34)=3.49, p=0.04).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta lateralisation data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: In experiment 2, there was a main effect of foreperiod on Mu/Beta lateralisation (F(3, 34)=3.49, p=0.04).
source: Similarly, we observed desynchronisation in Mu/Beta band activity over the hemispheres contralateral and ipsilateral to the response-executing hand throughout the pre-evidence foreperiod, with a progressive lateralisation toward the contralateral hemisphere on longer foreperiod trials (Figure 5i; 800 ms t(17)=-.40, p=0.69; 1200 ms: t(17)=-1.65, p=0.12; 1600 ms: t(17)=-3.23, p=0.005; main effect of foreperiod: F(3, 34)=3.49, p=0.04).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta lateralisation data.

claim: In experiment 2, the CPP amplitude prior to response did not vary significantly as a function of foreperiod duration (F(1.29, 21.92)=0.04, p=0.96).
source: Like experiment one the CPP amplitude prior to response did not vary significantly as a function of foreperiod duration (Figure 5c; F(1.29, 21.92)=0.04, p=0.96) or response time (Figure 5e; F(2, 34)=0.52, p=0.6).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP amplitude data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In experiment 2, the CPP amplitude prior to response did not vary significantly as a function of response time (F(2, 34)=0.52, p=0.6).
source: Like experiment one the CPP amplitude prior to response did not vary significantly as a function of foreperiod duration (Figure 5c; F(1.29, 21.92)=0.04, p=0.96) or response time (Figure 5e; F(2, 34)=0.52, p=0.6).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP amplitude data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: In experiment 2, the amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of foreperiod duration (F(2, 34)=0.13, p=0.88).
source: Likewise, the amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of foreperiod duration (Figure 5j; main effect foreperiod: F(2, 34)=0.13, p=0.88) or response time (Figure 5j; main effect response time: F(2, 34)=0.74, p=0.48).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta amplitude data shown in Figure 5j.

claim: In experiment 2, the amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of response time (F(2, 34)=0.74, p=0.48).
source: Likewise, the amplitude of contralateral Mu/Beta at the time of response did not vary as a function of foreperiod duration (Figure 5j; main effect foreperiod: F(2, 34)=0.13, p=0.88) or response time (Figure 5j; main effect response time: F(2, 34)=0.74, p=0.48).
evidence: Statistical analysis of Mu/Beta amplitude data.

claim: In experiment 2, there was significant sustained motion energy in the direction of the chosen response on fast RT trials (t(17)=2.21 p=0.04).
source: One-sample t-tests confirmed that there was significant sustained motion energy in the direction of the chosen response on fast RT trials (Figure 6a; t(17)=2.21 p=0.04) but not on slow RT trials (Figure 6a; t(17)=.03, p=0.98).
evidence: Statistical analysis of dot motion energy data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In experiment 2, there was no significant sustained motion energy in the direction of the chosen response on slow RT trials (t(17)=.03, p=0.98).
source: One-sample t-tests confirmed that there was significant sustained motion energy in the direction of the chosen response on fast RT trials (Figure 6a; t(17)=2.21 p=0.04) but not on slow RT trials (Figure 6a; t(17)=.03, p=0.98).
evidence: Statistical analysis of dot motion energy data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In experiment 2, there was significant pre-evidence build-up of the CPP on trials where the cumulative motion energy consistently favoured a particular choice (Amplitude: t(17)=3.21 p=0.005; Slope: t(17)=3.25, p=0.005).
source: We found that there was significant pre-evidence build-up of the CPP on trials where the cumulative motion energy consistently favoured a particular choice (Figure 6c; one-sample t-tests: Amplitude: t(17)=3.21 p=0.005; Slope: t(17)=3.25, p=0.005) but not on those where the dot motion weakly and/or inconsistently favoured a specific choice (Figure 6c; Amplitude vs 0: t(17)=1.37, p=0.19; Slope vs 0: t(17)=1.59, p=0.13).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: In experiment 2, there was no significant pre-evidence build-up of the CPP on trials where the dot motion weakly and/or inconsistently favoured a specific choice (Amplitude vs 0: t(17)=1.37, p=0.19; Slope vs 0: t(17)=1.59, p=0.13).
source: We found that there was significant pre-evidence build-up of the CPP on trials where the cumulative motion energy consistently favoured a particular choice (Figure 6c; one-sample t-tests: Amplitude: t(17)=3.21 p=0.005; Slope: t(17)=3.25, p=0.005) but not on those where the dot motion weakly and/or inconsistently favoured a specific choice (Figure 6c; Amplitude vs 0: t(17)=1.37, p=0.19; Slope vs 0: t(17)=1.59, p=0.13).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The build-up of the CPP in experiment 2 reflected cumulative motion energy during the foreperiod.
source: Paired samples t-tests comparing this pre-evidence CPP build-up between the two conditions (shallow vs steep pre-evidence motion integral) were significant (Amplitude: t(17)=2.41 p=0.03) or close-to-significant (Slope: t(17)=1.92, p=0.07) suggesting that the build-up of the CPP did reflect cumulative motion energy during the foreperiod.
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing CPP build-up between conditions.

claim: In experiment 1, behavioural performance on foreperiodn was modulated significantly by foreperiodn-1, such that responses were faster when foreperiodn-1 was shorter (F(2, 40)=140.17, p=2.49×10−19).
source: We found that behavioural performance on foreperiodn was modulated significantly by foreperiodn-1, such that responses were faster when foreperiodn-1 was shorter (Figure 7a; F(2, 40)=140.17, p=2.49×10−19) and this effect was more pronounced when foreperiodn was long (foreperiodn x foreperiodn-1 interaction: F(4, 80)=7.37, p=4.17×10−5).
evidence: Statistical analysis of sequential foreperiod effects shown in Figure 7a.

claim: In experiment 1, the effect of foreperiodn-1 on RT was more pronounced when foreperiodn was long (F(4, 80)=7.37, p=4.17×10−5).
source: We found that behavioural performance on foreperiodn was modulated significantly by foreperiodn-1, such that responses were faster when foreperiodn-1 was shorter (Figure 7a; F(2, 40)=140.17, p=2.49×10−19) and this effect was more pronounced when foreperiodn was long (foreperiodn x foreperiodn-1 interaction: F(4, 80)=7.37, p=4.17×10−5).
evidence: Statistical analysis of sequential foreperiod effects.

claim: In experiment 1, foreperiodn-1 affected accuracy (F(2, 40)=5.23, p=0.01), but this effect was dependent on foreperiodn (F(4, 80)=14.90, p=3.85×10−9).
source: Moreover, foreperiodn-1 also affected accuracy (F(2, 40)=5.23, p=0.01), but this effect was dependent on foreperiodn (foreperiodn x foreperiodn-1 interaction: F(4, 80)=14.90, p=3.85×10−9).
evidence: Statistical analysis of sequential foreperiod effects on accuracy.

claim: In experiment 1, on short or long foreperiodn trials, foreperiod repetition led to a gain in accuracy whereas a change in foreperiod duration from one trial to the next was associated with a cost to accuracy.
source: The trends shown in Figure 7b indicate that on short or long foreperiodn trials, foreperiod repetition led to a gain in accuracy whereas a change in foreperiod duration from one trial to the next was associated with a cost to accuracy.
evidence: Based on analysis of accuracy data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: In experiment 1, the rate of missed responses on short foreperiodn trials was reduced if short foreperiods occurred consecutively (F(2, 40)=36.51, p=9.52×10−10).
source: Furthermore, in line with the above effects, we found that the rate of missed responses on short foreperiodn trials was reduced if short foreperiods occurred consecutively (Figure 7c; F(2, 40)=36.51, p=9.52×10−10) while the rate of premature responses on long foreperiodn trials was reduced when long foreperiods occurred consecutively (Figure 7d; F(2, 40)=8.12, p=0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of missed response data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: In experiment 1, the rate of premature responses on long foreperiodn trials was reduced when long foreperiods occurred consecutively (F(2, 40)=8.12, p=0.001).
source: Furthermore, in line with the above effects, we found that the rate of missed responses on short foreperiodn trials was reduced if short foreperiods occurred consecutively (Figure 7c; F(2, 40)=36.51, p=9.52×10−10) while the rate of premature responses on long foreperiodn trials was reduced when long foreperiods occurred consecutively (Figure 7d; F(2, 40)=8.12, p=0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of premature response data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: In experiment 1, the CPP reached a higher amplitude at the time of the contrast change when foreperiodn-1 was shorter (F(2, 36)=4.38, p=0.02).
source: As illustrated in Figure 8a, the CPP reached a higher amplitude at the time of the contrast change when foreperiodn-1 was shorter (F(2, 36)=4.38, p=0.02).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CPP amplitude data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: In experiment 1, the pre-evidence amplitude differences in CPP arose from differences in the onset, rather than the rate, of premature evidence accumulation.
source: The absence of any effect of foreperiodn-1 on pre-evidence CPP slope (F(2, 36)=0.54, p=0.59) suggests that the pre-evidence amplitude differences arose from differences in the onset, rather than the rate, of premature evidence accumulation.
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis of CPP slope data.

claim: Decision onset timing is modulated by recent experience of temporal structure in the sensory environment.
source: Together these findings indicate that decision onset timing is modulated by recent experience of temporal structure in the sensory environment.
evidence: Summary inference from sequential foreperiod analyses.

claim: When evidence onsets are difficult to discern, participants initiate the accumulation of sensory information endogenously, before the actual evidence appears.
source: In this study we examined the effects of temporal uncertainty on evidence accumulation onset timing. Convergent behavioural and neurophysiological data reveal that when evidence onsets are difficult to discern, participants initiate the accumulation of sensory information endogenously, before the actual evidence appears.
evidence: Summary of main findings from both experiments.

claim: When sensory evidence onsets are unpredictable but relatively salient, early target selection signals are involved in triggering evidence accumulation onset.
source: Recent work has highlighted that when sensory evidence onsets are unpredictable but relatively salient, early target selection signals are involved in triggering evidence accumulation onset (Loughnane et al., 2016; see also Purcell et al., 2010; Purcell et al., 2012; Schall et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Participants adapted the onset timing of accumulation strategically, using their knowledge and recent experience of the underlying temporal structure of the task.
source: Importantly, and in line with the observations in Teichert et al. (2016), our data indicate that participants adapted the onset timing of accumulation strategically, using their knowledge and recent experience of the underlying temporal structure of the task.
evidence: Based on experimental findings and consistent with Teichert et al., 2016.

claim: Subjects in this study timed the onset of evidence accumulation to approximately coincide with the earliest possible time point at which evidence could be presented to them (800 ms).
source: For instance, the CPP data suggest that subjects in this study timed the onset of evidence accumulation to approximately coincide with the earliest possible time point at which evidence could be presented to them (800 ms).
evidence: Inference from CPP data analysis.

claim: The strategy of timing accumulation onset to the earliest possible evidence onset led to a peak in performance on intermediate foreperiod trials in experiment 1.
source: Rather than optimising overall performance on shorter foreperiod trials (which had a notably high rate of missed responses and earned the lowest number of points), this strategy instead led to a peak in performance on intermediate foreperiod trials (which had notably high levels of accuracy and low levels of both missed and premature responses thus earning a higher number of points).
evidence: Based on analysis of behavioral performance data.

claim: Subjects may have adopted a Bayesian approach, 'regression to the mean', in estimating the response deadline.
source: One speculative explanation for this is that subjects may have adopted a Bayesian approach, 'regression to the mean', in estimating the response deadline, (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010; Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2015).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations to Bayesian timing studies.

claim: The timing of evidence accumulation onset is, at least in part, calibrated based on the duration of the foreperiod on recent trials.
source: Here we show that the timing of evidence accumulation onset is, at least in part, calibrated based on the duration of the foreperiod on recent trials, with shorter foreperiods leading to earlier accumulation onset on subsequent trials and correspondingly faster RTs.
evidence: Based on sequential foreperiod analysis.

claim: Trial-by-trial adjustments in accumulation onset timing reflect continuous updating of temporal expectations that inform accumulation onset timing.
source: According to the normative theories, intertrial dependencies such as this may reflect the inherent tendency for the brain to monitor and exploit local statistical patterns in the environment in order to reduce uncertainty (Jones et al., 2013; Wilder et al., 2013; Wilder et al., 2010; Yu and Cohen, 2008). Thus, these trial-by-trial adjustments in accumulation onset timing may reflect continuous updating of temporal expectations that inform accumulation onset timing.
evidence: Inference based on normative theories cited.

claim: Early CPP build-up in experiment 2 was driven by random fluctuations in motion energy.
source: With regard to the precise nature of the evidence accumulated during the foreperiod on later onset trials, our data show that this, at least partly, reflects the accumulation of sensory noise. In experiment two, we were able to show that early CPP build-up was driven by random fluctuations in motion energy, which, on some trials, cumulatively favoured one choice or another.
evidence: Based on dot motion energy analysis in experiment 2.

claim: The sequential foreperiod effect can be attributed to the adjustment in evidence accumulation onset timing.
source: Our results replicate the sequential foreperiod effect using a task in which respondents performed a difficult perceptual discrimination task where the foreperiod varied pseudorandomly from trial to trial. In this context at least, the sequential foreperiod effect, the underlying mechanisms of which have not yet been fully explained, can be attributed to the adjustment in evidence accumulation onset timing.
evidence: Based on experimental findings and analysis of sequential foreperiod effects.

claim: Neural decision signals can be leveraged to gain insights into the timing of accumulation onset that are otherwise very difficult to discern through behaviour.
source: Finally, our study also highlights how neural decision signals can be leveraged to gain insights into the timing of accumulation onset that are otherwise very difficult to discern through behaviour.
evidence: Summary of methodological contribution of the study.

claim: It is possible to infer the timing of accumulation onset directly from the temporal dynamics of the CPP.
source: Our data highlight that it is possible to infer the timing of accumulation onset directly from the temporal dynamics of the CPP.
evidence: Based on CPP analysis throughout the study.

claim: In the absence of foreknowledge about the precise timing of a subtle goal relevant sensory change, observers are unable to accurately time the onset of sensory evidence accumulation with respect to that event.
source: Firstly, we have shown that in the absence of foreknowledge about the precise timing of a subtle goal relevant sensory change, observers are unable to accurately time the onset of sensory evidence accumulation with respect to that event, resulting in instances where accumulation commences too early, leading to premature responses and fast errors, as well as instances where accumulation is delayed, leading to missed responses.
evidence: Summary of key finding from the study.

claim: Accumulation onset timing is not governed solely by sensory driven mechanisms but instead can be controlled by top-down processes.
source: Secondly, we have demonstrated that accumulation onset timing is not governed solely by sensory driven mechanisms but instead can be controlled by top-down processes.
evidence: Summary of key finding from the study.

claim: We rely on and continuously update our average representation of the temporal structure of a given task.
source: To this end, we appear to rely on and continuously update our average representation of the temporal structure of a given task.
evidence: Summary conclusion from sequential foreperiod analysis.
